L1@P0: June 18, 2026
L2@P0: To: Honorable Mayor and Members of the City Council
L3@P0: From: Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
L4@P0: Re: Homeless Response Team Performance Data Report
L5@P0: Introduction
L6@P0: This Homeless Response Team (HRT) data report is the third in a series of biannual data
L7@P0: reports to the City Council, following the May 12, 2025 and November 7, 2025 memos.
L8@P0: The data reports provide consistent outcome measures over time, in line with the
L9@P0: recommendation of the City Auditor’s July 2025 audit of the HRT. With three reporting
L10@P0: periods now available, some outcome measures are beginning to show stability across
L11@P0: reports while others continue to vary in ways that likely reflect period-specific cohort
L12@P0: composition. The most operationally significant finding in this report is that, with new
L13@P0: shelter capacity that the City and County have brought online over the past year, 58% of
L14@P0: HRT participants achieved a shelter or housing outcome in this reporting period, with an
L15@P0: additional 31% actively engaged with the team but not yet placed.
L16@P0: Overview of Homeless Response Team
L17@P0: The Homeless Response Team is coordinated by the Neighborhood Services Division in
L18@P0: the City Manager’s Office, which coordinates a multi-departmental effort to address all of
L19@P0: the needs and impacts of the people who live in, work or visit the area of a particular
L20@P0: encampment. The effort also includes staff from Public Works, Health, Housing &
L21@P0: Community Services, City Attorney’s Office, Police, Fire and Parks, Recreation and
L22@P0: Waterfront, and other departments/divisions as needed.
L23@P0: Concerns about encampments are reported by community members (often through 311),
L24@P0: Councilmembers, merchants, or City Staff, including HRT. HRT staff will then assess the
L25@P0: site for its impacts, looking at several key domains, including community impacts, public
L26@P0: health and safety, and environmental considerations, to decide how and when to address
L27@P0: encampment concerns.
L28@P0: Encampments are then prioritized with these factors in mind to determine if an
L29@P0-1: intervention is warranted.Homeless Response Team Performance Data Report
L30@P1: June 18, 2026
L31@P1: Page 2
L32@P1: Key Takeaways
L33@P1: 1. Demographic indicators continue to vary report-to-report, while
L34@P1: vulnerability indicators remain consistently high.
L35@P1: This report represents the third snapshot using the revamped set of HRT outcome
L36@P1: measures introduced in May 2025. Some demographic indicators continue to fluctuate
L37@P1: from one reporting period to the next. The share of participants self-identifying as female
L38@P1: moved from 32% in May 2025 to 48% in November 2025 and 37% in this report. The
L39@P1: share self-reporting a substance use disorder moved from 62% to 87% to 79% over the
L40@P1: same three reports. These variations most likely reflect the specific composition of who
L41@P1: the HRT encountered during each six-month period rather than systemic trends, and HRT
L42@P1: staff will continue to monitor them.
L43@P1: What does appear stable, if not rising, across all three reports is the high level of
L44@P1: vulnerability among HRT participants. In this period, 97% of HRT participants selfreported having a disability (compared to 89% in November 2025 and 94% in May 2025),
L45@P1: and 93% self-reported a mental health disorder (compared to 87% in November 2025
L46@P1: and 81% in May 2025). Physical disability also rose meaningfully, with 76% of participants
L47@P1: self-reporting a physical disability this period (compared to 37% in November 2025 and
L48@P1: 56% in May 2025), likely reflecting the specific population the team encountered. Across
L49@P1: all three reports, HRT participants have consistently reported substantially higher rates of
L50@P1: vulnerability than the broader Alameda County homeless population captured in the 2024
L51@P1: federal Point-in-Time (PIT) Count.
L52@P1: 2. Berkeley remains the largest single source of HRT participants, but inflows
L53@P1: from neighboring jurisdictions are increasing.
L54@P1: Berkeley continues to be the top source of HRT participants on a cumulative basis.
L55@P1: However, the most recent six-month cohort shows meaningful inflows from neighboring
L56@P1: jurisdictions. Twenty-one new participants in this period self-reported Oakland as their
L57@P1: last city of residence prior to becoming homeless, compared to 17 from Berkeley. Sixteen
L58@P1: new participants reported Contra Costa County, and 14 reported other California
L59@P1: communities.
L60@P1: This regional pattern is consistent with what the HRT has been hearing from participants
L61@P1: in the field, and what a recent UCSF evaluation0F
L62@P1: 1 on Berkeley’s encampment efforts
L63@P1: corroborated: as neighboring cities undertake encampment clearances, displaced
L64@P1: individuals are increasingly arriving in Berkeley. The size and composition of Berkeley’s
L65@P1: 1 See: https://homelessness.ucsf.edu/sites/default/files/2026-
L66@P1-2: 03/Berkeley%20RV%20Interim%20Evaluation%20Final%203.31.pdfHomeless Response Team Performance Data Report
L67@P2: June 18, 2026
L68@P2: Page 3
L69@P2: unsheltered population is being shaped not only by local conditions but also by
L70@P2: encampment enforcement decisions in neighboring jurisdictions, which are outside the
L71@P2: City’s control.
L72@P2: 3. More HRT participants have accessed shelter in this reporting period than
L73@P2: in the previous report, with most HRT engagements leading to shelter,
L74@P2: housing, or continued engagement with the team.
L75@P2: 55% of HRT participants in this reporting period have enrolled in a shelter program at
L76@P2: some point during their engagement with the team (Attachment 1, slide 5), a significant
L77@P2: improvement from the 25% reported in November 2025. The increase reflects the
L78@P2: cumulative impact of new shelter capacity that the City and County have brought online,
L79@P2: particularly through the winter relief shelter beds operated by Dorothy Day House, new
L80@P2: respite beds brought online by the County, and ongoing openings at encampment
L81@P2: resolution funded beds.
L82@P2: Looking at HRT participant outcomes more broadly (Attachment 1, slide 8), 58% of
L83@P2: participants in this reporting period achieved a shelter or housing outcome, 31% are
L84@P2: actively engaged with the team but not yet placed, and 11% have disengaged from
L85@P2: services.
L86@P2: 4. Coordinated Entry assessment rates and PSH eligibility among HRT
L87@P2: participants remain strong; PSH placement remains a County-controlled
L88@P2: bottleneck.
L89@P2: 91% of HRT participants in this reporting period have received a Coordinated Entry
L90@P2: housing needs assessment, comparable to 94% in November 2025 and a significant
L91@P2: increase from 60% in May 2025. Of those assessed, approximately 84% scored at or
L92@P2: above the threshold for permanent supportive housing (PSH) eligibility (a score of 80 or
L93@P2: higher), with the majority concentrated in the 80–99 range.
L94@P2: The HRT continues to identify and engage participants who are most in need of intensive
L95@P2: housing support. However, PSH placement decisions are controlled by Alameda County,
L96@P2: not the City of Berkeley. The HRT can refer eligible participants to PSH but cannot directly
L97@P2: place them into housing. This structural constraint is reflected in the breakdown of
L98@P2: sheltered or housed outcomes (Attachment 1, slide 8, right-side chart): of HRT
L99@P2: participants who achieved a shelter or housing outcome in this period, 95% are in shelter
L100@P2: while only 5% have moved to permanent or temporary housing destinations, comparable
L101@P2-3: to prior reports.Homeless Response Team Performance Data Report
L102@P3: June 18, 2026
L103@P3: Page 4
L104@P3: Conclusion
L105@P3: Using State Encampment Resolution Fund dollars (leveraged by Measure P), the HRT
L106@P3: opened 4 noncongregate motel programs between 2022 and 2025—an average of one
L107@P3: new program per year. This rapid increase in interim housing stock helped move some of
L108@P3: Berkeley’s hardest-to-serve unsheltered population indoors. As reported by city staff in
L109@P3: September 16, 2025, work session presentation to the City Council1F
L110@P3: 2, the city faces a
L111@P3: significant general fund deficit and existing ERF noncongregate motels face a multimillion dollar fiscal cliff over the coming years. Altogether, as funding priorities shift to
L112@P3: addressing funding gaps in current shelter programs, the current fiscal climate will make
L113@P3: it challenging to open new shelter programs without additional grant funding or other
L114@P3: outside resources. Without expanding shelter and housing capacity, the current rate of
L115@P3: HRT placement documented in this report cannot be sustained, and a decline in positive
L116@P3: outcomes is likely over time.
L117@P3: All of this speaks to the continued need to partner with and advocate to Alameda County
L118@P3: so that Berkeley receives an appropriate share of Measure W sales tax funding to support
L119@P3: the continuation of existing programs and development of new ones. City staff are
L120@P3: currently engaged with County counterparts in the Measure W administrative planning
L121@P3: process, advocating for Berkeley’s needs in the homeless system of care.

L3@P0: From: Paul Buddenhagen, City Manager
L4@P0: Re: New Homeless Response Team Mission and Performance Data Report
L5@P0: Introduction:
L6@P0: This memorandum presents a new mission statement for the Homeless Response
L7@P0: Team (HRT), and provides the first in a series of data reports that will measure progress
L8@P0: towards that mission.
L9@P0: The new mission statement is more reflective of the team’s ongoing commitment to
L10@P0: resolving encampments through coordinated efforts and service-forward interventions:
L11@P0: The Homeless Response Team’s mission is to resolve unsheltered
L12@P0: homelessness through the provision of interim and permanent housing and other
L13@P0: supportive services, as well as to coordinate the many City and nonprofit staff
L14@P0: who work in and are impacted by homeless encampments in providing harmreduction oriented, pragmatic interventions that maintain health and safety for the
L15@P0: unsheltered and the broader Berkeley community.
L16@P0: On June 4, 2024, the Homeless Response Team (HRT) sent an Off-Agenda Memo to
L17@P0: the City Council, presenting the first of a series of data reports quantifying the team’s
L18@P0: work.0F

L22@P0: Information System (HMIS) to perform Coordinated Entry housing assessments.1F
L23@P0: 2 The

L33@P1: Background:
L34@P1: In July 2021, the City Council adopted the All Home Regional Action plan2F
L35@P1: 3, and by
L36@P1: doing so, set the ambitious goal of achieving a 75% reduction in street homelessness
L37@P1: within three years (2024). This goal became the primary mission of the HRT.
L38@P1: The Homeless Response Team was launched in September of 2021. With no national
L39@P1: best-practice standards for the best way to track, quantify, and present data on the
L40@P1: complex work of homeless encampment management and resolution (itself a new field
L41@P1: with minimal Federal guidance or academic research, especially in 2021),
L42@P1: Neighborhood Services identified three performance metrics for the community at the
L43@P1: time, and developed its own rudimentary data-tracking systems to capture and measure
L44@P1: its work.
L45@P1: The City achieved a remarkable 45% reduction in street homelessness since that time,
L46@P1: but with the initial three-year deadline of the All Home Regional Action Plan having
L47@P1: passed, new goals for the HRT have not yet been set. Moreover, because the
L48@P1: Homeless Response Team has fully transitioned to use of the HMIS, it is possible to
L49@P1: perform more robust analysis of the people served by the team and their outcomes.
L50@P1: New Data Report Design:
L51@P1: The data report provided in this memo (see Attachment 1) assesses progress towards
L52@P1: the first part of this mission, which is the resolution of unsheltered homelessness
L53@P1: (chiefly large and/or dangerous encampments) through the provision of shelter, housing
L54@P1: or services. Key HRT findings include:
L55@P1: 1. HRT participants are far more vulnerable than Alameda County’s homeless
L56@P1: population overall
L57@P1: 2. HRT participants are more likely to accept a noncongregate shelter bed than a
L58@P1: congregate shelter bed
L59@P1: 3. HRT participants are getting assessed for housing – and over 4 in 5 are eligible
L60@P1: for the most intensive housing resource in the homeless system of care
L61@P1: 4. Nearly 2/3 of HRT participants move indoors as a result of HRT intervention
L62@P1: 3 See: https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2021-07-

L66@P2: Findings of Interest:
L67@P2: 1. HRT participants are far more vulnerable than Alameda County’s homeless
L68@P2: population overall
L69@P2: Figure 1:
L70@P2: The chart above (Figure 1) illustrates a stark contrast between HRT's participants and
L71@P2: the broader County homeless population (according to the 2024 federal Point-in-Time or
L72@P2: PIT Count) for key vulnerability indicators. The data in the chart above result from selfreports, suggesting that they may actually be undercounts, given the sensitive and
L73@P2: highly personal nature of the questions. Across four of the five categories—disability,
L74@P2: mental health, substance use, physical disability, and HIV/AIDS—HRT participants
L75@P2: report significantly higher rates of vulnerability than were reported by PIT Count survey
L76@P2: participants. In the remaining category of HIV/AIDS, both the county and the HRT team
L77@P2: saw 3% of participants as being HIV+. Here are some key takeaways:
L78@P2: • 94% of HRT clients report having a disability, compared to just 60% of those in
L79@P2: the Alameda County PIT count.
L80@P2: • Mental health disorders are reported by over 80% of HRT participants, more than
L81@P2: double the county rate (35%).
L82@P2: • Substance use disorders affect 62% of HRT clients, compared to only 29%
L83@P2: countywide.

L109@P3: These disparities emphasize that the population served by HRT is not only experiencing
L110@P3: homelessness but is doing so with a significantly higher burden of complex health and
L111@P3: social needs. These data underscore the need for tailored, high-intensity interventions
L112@P3: and supports that address not just housing, but the full spectrum of client vulnerabilities.
L113@P3: It also demonstrates the huge task faced by the HRT in executing its mission to reduce
L114@P3: unsheltered homelessness.
L115@P3: 2. HRT participants are more likely to accept a noncongregate shelter bed than a
L116@P3: congregate shelter bed
L117@P3: Figure 2: Figure 3:
L118@P3: Figure 2 above illustrates the individuals enrolled in the HRT program who also enrolled
L119@P3: into a Berkeley emergency shelter. Participants must be enrolled in both programs to be
L120@P3: counted. Participants are enrolled into the HRT program if the HRT provides a service
L121@P3: (Coordinated Entry Assessment, shelter referral, job training referral, etc.) to that
L122@P3: participant. Participants are enrolled into a shelter program after they complete the
L123@P3: intake process. Data for the 301 participants analyzed, since the inception of the HRT
L124@P3: in September 2021, show that 206 (68%) entered noncongregate shelters, while only 95
L125@P3: (32%) accessed congregate shelter options. This is true despite only 25% of shelter
L126@P3: beds in Berkeley being noncongregate (Figure 3 above).
L127@P3: The clear preference for noncongregate placements reflects what we continue to
L128@P3: hear from participants: privacy, safety, and autonomy matter—especially for
L129@P3: individuals managing complex health or trauma histories. Importantly, data suggest
L130@P3: that noncongregate programs are more successful than congregate programs in
L131@P3: actually ending homelessness: since 2022 with the launch of the Rodeway to Home (the
L132@P3: city’s first directly contracted noncongregate shelter), 34% of people in noncongregate
L133@P3: shelters have moved directly into permanent housing, versus 22% for congregate
L134@P3: shelters.

L152@P4: In recent years, staff from the Neighborhood Services Division in the City Manager’s
